stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. The magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from the wire is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: For a long straight wire B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/0.02 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T. Using 1 cm instead of 2 cm gives 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ T, and using the loop formula μ₀I/(2r) gives 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ T; neither applies to a straight wire at 2 cm.

stem: The magnetic field lines around a long straight current-carrying wire are
options: Lines radially outward from the wire
explanation: The field of a straight current forms closed concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire, with direction given by the right-hand grip rule. Radial lines describe the electric field of a line charge, not the magnetic field of a current.

stem: A solenoid 50 cm long has 500 turns and carries a current of 4 A. The magnetic field inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: Turns per metre n = 500/0.5 = 1000 m⁻¹, so B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000 × 4 = 1.6π × 10⁻³ T. Using N = 500 directly instead of turns per metre gives 0.8π × 10⁻³ T, and dividing by 50 cm without converting to metres gives 1.6π × 10⁻⁵ T.

stem: A closed loop encloses two long parallel wires carrying currents of 3 A and 5 A in opposite directions. The magnitude of ∮B·dL around the loop is
explanation: Ampere's law gives ∮B·dL = μ₀ × (net current enclosed). The currents are opposite, so the net current is 5 − 3 = 2 A and the integral is 2μ₀ T m. Adding the currents to get 8μ₀ ignores their directions.

stem: The number of turns per unit length of a long solenoid is doubled and the current through it is halved. The magnetic field inside the solenoid
explanation: B = μ₀nI depends on the product nI. Doubling n and halving I leaves nI, and so B, unchanged. Choosing 'four times' wrongly treats both changes as increases.

stem: A straight wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T. The force on the wire is
explanation: F = BIL sin θ = 0.2 × 4 × 0.5 × sin 90° = 0.4 N. The answer 0.8 N comes from forgetting the factor 0.5 m for the length.

stem: A wire 0.8 m long carrying 5 A lies in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T, making an angle of 30° with the field. The magnitude of the force on it is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
explanation: F = BIL sin θ = 0.5 × 5 × 0.8 × sin 30° = 2.0 × 0.5 = 1.0 N. Using cos 30° instead of sin 30° gives about 1.7 N; the angle in BIL sin θ is between the wire and the field.

stem: Two long parallel wires 5 cm apart each carry 10 A in the same direction. The force per metre between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 10/0.05 = 4 × 10⁻⁴ N/m. Parallel currents in the same direction attract; only opposite currents repel.

stem: A horizontal wire of mass 0.02 kg per metre lies at right angles to a horizontal magnetic field of 0.5 T. The current needed for the magnetic force to support its weight is (g = 10 m/s²)
explanation: For balance BIL = mg, so I = (m/L)g/B = 0.02 × 10/0.5 = 0.4 A. Forgetting g gives 0.04 A, which supports only a tenth of the weight.

stem: A coil of 100 turns and area 20 cm² carries 0.5 A in a uniform field of 0.4 T, with the plane of the coil parallel to the field. The torque on the coil is
explanation: With the plane parallel to B the torque is maximum: τ = NIAB = 100 × 0.5 × 20 × 10⁻⁴ × 0.4 = 0.04 N m. 'Zero' is the torque when the plane is perpendicular to the field, and 0.4 N m comes from taking 20 cm² as 2 × 10⁻² m².

stem: A rectangular coil of 50 turns and area 0.01 m² carries 2 A in a uniform field of 0.2 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the field. The torque on the coil is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
explanation: τ = NIAB cos α, where α is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field: 50 × 2 × 0.01 × 0.2 × cos 60° = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.10 N m. Using sin 60° gives 0.17 N m, which treats 60° as the angle between the field and the coil's normal.

stem: The force on a straight current-carrying conductor in a uniform magnetic field is maximum when the conductor is
explanation: F = BIL sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, that is θ = 90°. Parallel or antiparallel conductors have sin θ = 0 and feel no force at all.

stem: An electron moves at 2 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. The magnetic force on it is (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
explanation: F = qvB sin 90° = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10⁶ × 0.5 = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ N. Omitting the factor 0.5 for B gives 3.2 × 10⁻¹³ N.

stem: A charged particle moves through a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on the particle
explanation: F = q(v × B) is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed and kinetic energy stay constant; only the direction changes. The force is proportional to q, so it does depend on the charge.

stem: A particle of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C enters a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T at right angles with speed 2 × 10⁶ m/s. The radius of its circular path is
explanation: r = mv/(qB) = (1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.1) = 3.2 × 10⁻²¹/1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ = 0.2 m. Dropping the factor 0.1 of B in the denominator gives 0.02 m.

stem: A proton and an alpha particle enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles with the same speed. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton is
explanation: r = mv/(qB), so r ∝ m/q at equal speed. The alpha particle has 4 times the mass and 2 times the charge, so r_α/r_p = 4/2 = 2. Answer 1/2 inverts the ratio.

stem: A proton and an alpha particle with the same kinetic energy move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field. The ratio of the radius of the alpha particle's path to that of the proton is
explanation: With momentum p = √(2mK), r = √(2mK)/(qB) ∝ √m/q at equal K. For the alpha particle √4/2 = 1 relative to the proton's √1/1 = 1, so the ratio is 1. The answer 2 holds for equal speeds, not equal kinetic energies.

stem: A charged particle moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, the time it takes for one revolution
explanation: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB), which does not depend on speed. Doubling v doubles the radius, and the longer path exactly cancels the higher speed, so 'halved' is wrong.

stem: In a velocity selector, crossed fields E = 3 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.2 T are used. The speed of the ions that pass through undeflected is
explanation: Undeflected ions have qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 3 × 10⁴/0.2 = 1.5 × 10⁵ m/s. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 6.0 × 10³ m/s, and B/E gives 6.7 × 10⁻⁶ m/s.

stem: In an e/m experiment, electrons accelerated from rest through 250 V move in a circle of radius 5 cm in a uniform magnetic field of 1.0 × 10⁻³ T. The value of e/m obtained is
explanation: From eV = ½mv² and r = mv/(eB), e/m = 2V/(B²r²) = 500/(10⁻⁶ × 25 × 10⁻⁴) = 500/(2.5 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg. Dropping the factor 2 gives 1.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg, and treating 5 cm as the diameter gives 8.0 × 10¹¹ C/kg.

stem: A charged particle is projected parallel to a uniform magnetic field. Its path is a
explanation: For v parallel to B, F = qvB sin 0° = 0, so the particle continues in a straight line at constant velocity. A circle needs v perpendicular to B, and a helix needs an angle between 0° and 90°.

stem: An electron enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity at 30° to the field direction. Its path in the field is
explanation: The velocity component v cos 30° along B is unaffected, while the component v sin 30° perpendicular to B produces circular motion. The combination is a helix. A parabola would need a constant force in a fixed direction, as in an electric field.

stem: A circular coil of 10 turns and radius 10 cm carries a current of 2 A. The magnetic field at its centre is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: At the centre of a circular coil B = μ₀NI/(2R) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 2/(2 × 0.1) = 4π × 10⁻⁵ T. Using the diameter 0.2 m as R gives half this, 2π × 10⁻⁵ T.

stem: Two long parallel wires 10 cm apart carry 5 A each in opposite directions. The magnetic field at the point midway between them is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: Each wire gives B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 5/0.05 = 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at the midpoint. With opposite currents the two fields point the same way between the wires and add to 4 × 10⁻⁵ T. 'Zero' is the result for currents in the same direction.

stem: A moving coil galvanometer is converted into an ammeter by connecting
explanation: An ammeter must carry the large circuit current while only the small full-scale current passes through the coil, so a low resistance (shunt) is placed in parallel to divert the rest. A high resistance in series is the voltmeter conversion.

stem: To convert a galvanometer into a voltmeter, we connect
explanation: A voltmeter must draw very little current, so a high resistance is added in series; the full-scale current then flows only when the chosen maximum voltage is applied. A low parallel resistance would turn it into an ammeter.

stem: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives full-scale deflection for 10 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0-1 A is
explanation: The shunt carries I − Ig = 1 − 0.01 = 0.99 A at the same p.d. as the coil: S = IgG/(I − Ig) = 0.01 × 99/0.99 = 1 Ω. Dividing by the full 1 A instead of 0.99 A gives the tempting 0.99 Ω.

stem: A galvanometer has resistance 100 Ω and gives full-scale deflection at 1 mA. The resistance needed in series to make it a voltmeter of range 0-10 V is
explanation: The total resistance must be V/Ig = 10/0.001 = 10000 Ω, so the series resistance is 10000 − 100 = 9900 Ω. Choosing 10000 Ω forgets that the coil's own 100 Ω is already part of the total.

stem: A galvanometer of resistance 45 Ω is shunted by a 5 Ω resistor. The fraction of the total current that passes through the galvanometer is
explanation: Parallel branches share current inversely to resistance: Ig/I = S/(G + S) = 5/(45 + 5) = 1/10. The value 1/9 is the ratio of the two branch currents, Ig/Is = 5/45, not the fraction of the total.

stem: A voltmeter of range 0-5 V has a resistance of 1000 Ω. The extra resistance needed in series to extend its range to 0-20 V is
explanation: Full-scale current is 5/1000 = 5 mA. For 20 V the total resistance must be 20/0.005 = 4000 Ω, so the extra series resistance is 4000 − 1000 = 3000 Ω. The answer 4000 Ω is the new total, not the addition.

stem: An ideal voltmeter should have
options: a resistance equal to the circuit's
explanation: A voltmeter is connected in parallel and should take no current from the circuit, so its ideal resistance is infinite. Zero resistance is the ideal for an ammeter, which is connected in series.

stem: The current sensitivity of a moving coil galvanometer can be increased by
options: increasing the area of the coil
explanation: Deflection θ = NBA I/c, so θ/I rises with larger N, B or A and with a smaller torsional constant c. A stiffer suspension increases c and reduces the sensitivity.

stem: In a moving coil galvanometer, concave pole pieces and a soft iron core give a radial magnetic field so that
options: the coil stays cool at large currents
the restoring torque is cancelled out
the deflection is proportional to current
the coil's resistance is kept very low
explanation: In a radial field the plane of the coil is always parallel to B, so the deflecting torque NIAB does not depend on the angle and θ = NBAI/c is proportional to I, giving a linear scale. The restoring torque of the suspension is still needed to balance it.

stem: The range of an ammeter made from a galvanometer of resistance G is to be 10 times the galvanometer's full-scale current. The shunt resistance required is
explanation: With I = 10Ig, the shunt carries 9Ig at the same p.d.: S × 9Ig = G × Ig, so S = G/9. G/10 would make the range 11 times Ig.

stem: Two 2000 Ω resistors are connected in series with a 12 V cell of negligible internal resistance. A voltmeter of resistance 2000 Ω is connected across one of the resistors. The voltmeter reads
explanation: The voltmeter and the resistor in parallel give 1000 Ω, so the total is 3000 Ω and the current is 12/3000 = 4 mA. The p.d. across the parallel pair is 4 mA × 1000 Ω = 4 V. The answer 6 V is what an ideal voltmeter would read; a real voltmeter loads the circuit.

stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule for a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field, the thumb points along the
explanation: With the forefinger along the field and the middle finger along the current, the thumb gives the direction of motion, that is the force on the conductor. The induced emf belongs to the right-hand (dynamo) rule.

stem: An electron moves towards the east in a uniform magnetic field directed vertically upward. The magnetic force on the electron is directed towards the
explanation: For a positive charge v × B with v east and B up gives south (east × up = south). The electron is negative, so the force is reversed and points north. Choosing south forgets the negative charge.

stem: A proton moves towards the north in a uniform magnetic field directed towards the west. The magnetic force on the proton is directed
explanation: F = q(v × B) with v north and B west. Taking east = x, north = y, up = z: y × (−x) = −(y × x) = +z, so the force on the positive proton is vertically upward. The force must be perpendicular to both v and B, which rules out east and south.

stem: One tesla is equal to
explanation: From F = BIL, B = F/(IL), so 1 T = 1 N/(1 A × 1 m) = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ (also 1 Wb m⁻²). The other combinations do not follow from F = BIL.

stem: A uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T passes through a flat surface of area 0.05 m². The normal to the surface makes an angle of 60° with the field. The magnetic flux through the surface is
explanation: Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal: 0.4 × 0.05 × cos 60° = 0.02 × 0.5 = 0.01 Wb. The value 0.02 Wb ignores the angle, and 0.017 Wb uses sin 60°.

stem: A coil of area 0.5 m² is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.2 T so that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 30° with the field. The flux through one turn is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
explanation: If the plane makes 30° with B, the normal makes 60° with B, so Φ = BA cos 60° = 0.2 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.05 Wb. Using cos 30° gives 0.087 Wb, which mistakes the plane for the normal.

stem: The weber, the SI unit of magnetic flux, is equivalent to
explanation: Faraday's law ε = −ΔΦ/Δt gives the unit of flux as volt × second, so 1 Wb = 1 V s (also 1 T m²). V A is the watt and A s is the coulomb.

stem: In a mass spectrometer, singly charged ions of masses 20 u and 22 u enter the same magnetic field at right angles with the same speed. The lighter ions move in a circle of radius 10 cm. The radius for the heavier ions is
explanation: r = mv/(qB), so with equal v, q and B the radius is proportional to mass: r = 10 × 22/20 = 11 cm. The value 12.1 cm wrongly assumes r ∝ m².

stem: An electron (mass mₑ) and a proton (mass mₚ) are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference and then enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles. The ratio of the radius of the proton's path to that of the electron is
explanation: Both gain kinetic energy eV, so momentum p = √(2meV) and r = p/(eB) ∝ √m since the charges have equal magnitude. Hence rₚ/rₑ = √(mₚ/mₑ). The ratio mₚ/mₑ would apply only if both had the same speed.

stem: A particle of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. Its angular velocity is
explanation: From qvB = mv²/r, ω = v/r = qB/m = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.5/1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ = 5.0 × 10⁷ rad/s. The value 8.0 × 10⁶ is the frequency f = ω/2π in hertz, not the angular velocity.

stem: The magnetic field well inside a long current-carrying solenoid is
explanation: Inside a long solenoid the fields of the turns combine into a uniform field B = μ₀nI parallel to the axis. Circular field lines around an axis describe a straight wire or a toroid, not the inside of a solenoid.

stem: The magnetic field at 6 cm from a long straight current-carrying wire is 3 × 10⁻⁵ T. The field at 2 cm from the same wire is
explanation: B = μ₀I/(2πr) ∝ 1/r, so reducing r from 6 cm to 2 cm triples the field to 9 × 10⁻⁵ T. The value 27 × 10⁻⁵ T assumes an inverse-square law, which applies to a point charge's electric field, not a wire's magnetic field.

stem: An alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 5 × 10⁵ m/s at 30° to a magnetic field of 0.4 T. The magnetic force on it is
explanation: F = qvB sin θ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10⁵ × 0.4 × 0.5 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Leaving out sin 30° gives 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, and using cos 30° gives about 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ N.

stem: The magnetic flux through each turn of a 200-turn coil falls from 0.05 Wb to 0.01 Wb in 0.2 s. The average emf induced in the coil is
explanation: ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 200 × (0.05 − 0.01)/0.2 = 200 × 0.04/0.2 = 40 V. Leaving out N gives 0.2 V, and adding the two flux values instead of subtracting gives 60 V.

stem: Lenz's law is a consequence of the law of conservation of
explanation: The induced current always opposes the change that produces it, so work must be done against it and that work appears as electrical energy. If the induced current aided the change, energy would be created from nothing, violating conservation of energy.

stem: A straight rod 0.5 m long moves at 4 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.3 T, with the rod perpendicular to both its velocity and the field. The emf induced across its ends is
explanation: Motional emf ε = BLv = 0.3 × 0.5 × 4 = 0.6 V. Leaving out the speed gives BL = 0.15 V, but the emf grows in proportion to how fast the rod cuts the field.

stem: A rod 0.2 m long slides at a constant 5 m/s on two parallel rails in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T perpendicular to the plane of the rails. The total resistance of the circuit is 2 Ω. The external force needed to keep the rod moving at constant speed is
explanation: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.2 × 5 = 0.5 V, so I = 0.5/2 = 0.25 A. The magnetic force opposing the motion is BIL = 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.2 = 0.025 N, and the applied force must equal it. The answer 0.25 N is the current in amperes, not a force.

stem: A conducting rod 0.4 m long moves at 10 m/s on rails at right angles to a magnetic field of 0.5 T. The circuit has a total resistance of 4 Ω. The rate at which heat is produced in the circuit is
explanation: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.4 × 10 = 2 V and P = ε²/R = 4/4 = 1 W. Taking the current ε/R = 0.5 A as the power gives 0.5 W, and forgetting to divide ε² by R gives 4 W; the mechanical power supplied, Fv, also equals 1 W.

stem: The north pole of a bar magnet is pushed towards one face of a closed coil. As the magnet approaches, that face of the coil behaves as
options: a south pole, attracting the magnet
a north pole, repelling the magnet
a north pole, attracting the magnet
a south pole, repelling the magnet
explanation: By Lenz's law the induced current opposes the approach, so the near face becomes a north pole and repels the incoming north pole. A south pole would attract the magnet and increase the change, which would create energy from nothing.

stem: A strong bar magnet is dropped vertically through a long vertical copper tube. While inside the tube, its acceleration is
explanation: The falling magnet changes the flux through the tube walls, inducing eddy currents whose magnetic field opposes its motion (Lenz's law). This retarding force makes its acceleration less than g; it is not zero at the start because the magnet begins at rest with no induced current.

stem: The henry, the SI unit of inductance, is equal to
explanation: From ε = L ΔI/Δt, L = ε Δt/ΔI, so 1 H = 1 V s A⁻¹ (also 1 Wb A⁻¹). Wb A multiplies instead of dividing by the current.

stem: The current in a coil of self-inductance 0.2 H falls steadily from 5 A to 1 A in 0.1 s. The magnitude of the self-induced emf is
explanation: ε = L ΔI/Δt = 0.2 × (5 − 1)/0.1 = 0.2 × 40 = 8 V. Adding the currents gives 12 V, and leaving out L gives 40 V.

stem: A steady current of 4 A flows through an inductor of 0.5 H. The energy stored in its magnetic field is
explanation: U = ½LI² = ½ × 0.5 × 16 = 4 J. Forgetting the factor ½ gives 8 J, and forgetting to square I gives 1 J.

stem: When the current through an inductor is increased from 2 A to 4 A, the energy stored in it increases by 6 J. The inductance is
explanation: ΔU = ½L(I₂² − I₁²) = ½L(16 − 4) = 6L = 6 J, so L = 1 H. Using (ΔI)² = 4 instead of the difference of squares gives 3 H, and omitting the ½ gives 0.5 H.

stem: The mutual inductance between two coils is 0.3 H. If the current in the primary changes at a rate of 20 A/s, the emf induced in the secondary is
explanation: ε = M ΔI/Δt = 0.3 × 20 = 6 V. Dividing the rate by M gives 66.7 V, which has the wrong dependence: a larger mutual inductance gives a larger emf.

stem: The self-induced emf in a coil always opposes
options: the steady current through the coil
any change in the current through it
the resistance of the coil's wire
the terminal voltage of the source
explanation: ε = −L ΔI/Δt exists only while the current changes and acts against that change, as Lenz's law requires. With a steady current there is no self-induced emf at all.

stem: A solenoid 0.5 m long has 1000 turns and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm². Its self-inductance is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: L = μ₀N²A/l = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10⁶ × 10⁻³/0.5 = 8π × 10⁻⁴ H. Using N instead of N² gives 8π × 10⁻⁷ H, and taking 10 cm² as 0.1 m² gives 8π × 10⁻² H.

stem: A long solenoid is rewound with twice the number of turns over the same length and cross-section. Its self-inductance becomes
explanation: L = μ₀N²A/l, so doubling N multiplies L by 2² = 4. 'Double' forgets that N enters twice: once in the field B = μ₀NI/l and once in the flux linkage NΦ.

stem: According to Faraday's law, the emf induced in a coil is proportional to
options: the rate of change of flux
explanation: ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt: the emf depends on how fast the flux linkage changes, not on the flux itself. A large but steady flux induces no emf.

stem: A circular loop lies in the plane of the page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. If the field is increasing, the induced current in the loop, as seen by a viewer facing the page, is
explanation: The inward flux is increasing, so the induced current must produce a field out of the page inside the loop. By the right-hand grip rule that current is anticlockwise. A clockwise current would add to the inward flux.

stem: A coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m² is in a uniform field of 0.5 T with its plane perpendicular to the field. It is turned in 0.1 s until its plane is parallel to the field. The average emf induced is
explanation: The flux per turn falls from BA = 0.5 × 0.02 = 0.01 Wb to zero, so ε = NΔΦ/Δt = 100 × 0.01/0.1 = 10 V. The value 20 V would apply to a half-turn, where the flux reverses from +BA to −BA.

stem: The flux through each turn of a 50-turn coil of total resistance 10 Ω changes by 0.02 Wb. The charge that flows through the coil is
explanation: I = ε/R = NΔΦ/(RΔt), so the charge q = IΔt = NΔΦ/R = 50 × 0.02/10 = 0.1 C, independent of how fast the change happens. Leaving out N gives 0.002 C.

stem: A metal rod 0.5 m long rotates at 20 rad/s about one end in a plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T. The emf between the ends of the rod is
explanation: Points on the rod move at speeds from 0 to ωL, so the average speed is ωL/2 and ε = ½BωL² = ½ × 0.4 × 20 × 0.25 = 1.0 V. Using the tip speed ωL for the whole rod gives 2.0 V.

stem: The iron core of a transformer is made of thin insulated laminations in order to
explanation: Thin insulated sheets break the large closed paths in which eddy currents would circulate, so the heating loss in the core falls sharply. Laminating does not increase the flux linkage, which depends on the core material and the windings.

stem: A straight conductor 1 m long moves at 2 m/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The conductor is perpendicular to both the field and its velocity, and the velocity makes 30° with the field. The emf induced is (√3 ≈ 1.73)
explanation: Only the velocity component perpendicular to B cuts the field lines: ε = BLv sin θ = 0.5 × 1 × 2 × sin 30° = 0.5 V. Ignoring the angle gives 1.0 V, and using cos 30° gives 0.87 V.

stem: An aircraft with a wingspan of 40 m flies horizontally at 250 m/s where the vertical component of the Earth's magnetic field is 5 × 10⁻⁵ T. The emf between its wing tips is
explanation: The wings cut the vertical component of the field: ε = BLv = 5 × 10⁻⁵ × 40 × 250 = 0.5 V. Slipping a power of ten in 5 × 10⁻⁵ gives 0.05 V or 5 V.

stem: A current of 2 A in a primary coil produces a flux of 4 × 10⁻⁴ Wb through each of the 500 turns of a nearby secondary coil. The mutual inductance of the pair is
explanation: M = NₛΦₛ/Iₚ = 500 × 4 × 10⁻⁴/2 = 0.1 H. Multiplying by the current instead of dividing gives 0.4 H, and leaving out the 500 turns gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ H.

stem: A generator coil of 100 turns and area 0.02 m² rotates at an angular speed of 50 rad/s in a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The peak emf generated is
explanation: For a rotating coil ε = NABω sin ωt, so the peak value is ε₀ = NABω = 100 × 0.02 × 0.5 × 50 = 50 V. Halving it to 25 V confuses the peak with an average-type value.

stem: An AC generator works on the principle of
explanation: Rotating the coil in a magnetic field changes the flux linked with it, inducing an emf by Faraday's law. The motor effect, the force on a current in a field, is the principle of the motor, the reverse device.

stem: In an AC generator, the emf induced in the rotating coil is maximum at the instant when the plane of the coil is
explanation: ε = NABω sin ωt is largest when the flux through the coil is zero but changing fastest, which happens when the plane of the coil is parallel to B. When the plane is perpendicular to B the flux is maximum but momentarily not changing, so the emf is zero.

stem: The speed of rotation of an AC generator's coil is doubled. The effect on the peak emf and on the frequency is
explanation: Peak emf ε₀ = NABω and frequency f = ω/2π are both proportional to ω, so both double. The emf does not rise four times because ω appears only once in NABω.

stem: In a DC motor, the split-ring commutator
options: reverses the coil current every half turn
reduces the resistance of the coil
changes the mains AC into steady DC
explanation: Every half rotation the commutator reverses the current in the coil, so the torque keeps acting in the same sense and the coil turns continuously. It does not change the field or the coil's resistance.

stem: A DC motor connected to a 220 V supply has an armature resistance of 2 Ω and draws 10 A when running normally. The back emf is
explanation: V = ε_b + IR, so ε_b = 220 − 10 × 2 = 200 V. The value 20 V is only the drop across the armature resistance, and 240 V adds that drop instead of subtracting it.

stem: A DC motor with armature resistance 4 Ω runs on 120 V and develops a back emf of 100 V at full speed. The current at the instant of switching on is
explanation: At switch-on the armature is at rest, so there is no back emf and I = V/R = 120/4 = 30 A. The value 5 A is the running current (120 − 100)/4, which flows only once the back emf has built up.

stem: A DC motor works on 200 V, has an armature resistance of 5 Ω and draws 4 A at full speed. Ignoring friction, the mechanical power it develops is
explanation: Back emf ε_b = 200 − 4 × 5 = 180 V, and the mechanical power is ε_b I = 180 × 4 = 720 W. The input is VI = 800 W, of which I²R = 80 W is wasted as heat, so 800 W is not the output.

stem: A DC motor is suddenly given a heavier load, so it slows down. As a result
options: back emf rises and current falls
both back emf and current fall
both back emf and current rise
back emf falls and current rises
explanation: Back emf is proportional to the speed, so it falls when the motor slows. Since I = (V − ε_b)/R, the current rises and supplies the extra torque. This is why an overloaded or stalled motor can overheat.

stem: A transformer does not work with a steady DC supply because
options: DC heats the core too much
DC flows only in the secondary
explanation: A transformer relies on mutual induction, which needs a changing flux in the core. A steady direct current gives a constant flux, so no emf is induced in the secondary.

stem: An ideal transformer has 100 turns on the primary and 2000 turns on the secondary. If the primary is connected to 220 V AC, the secondary voltage is
explanation: Vₛ/Vₚ = Nₛ/Nₚ = 2000/100 = 20, so Vₛ = 20 × 220 = 4400 V. Inverting the turns ratio gives 11 V, which would be a step-down transformer.

stem: An ideal transformer steps 220 V down to 11 V. The secondary supplies a current of 4 A. The primary current is
explanation: For an ideal transformer VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ, so Iₚ = 11 × 4/220 = 0.2 A. Multiplying by the voltage ratio the wrong way gives 80 A; a step-down transformer has a smaller current in its primary.

stem: A transformer of efficiency 90% steps 240 V down to 12 V. The secondary supplies 9 A to a load. The primary current is
explanation: Output power = 12 × 9 = 108 W, so the input power is 108/0.9 = 120 W and Iₚ = 120/240 = 0.5 A. Ignoring the efficiency gives 108/240 = 0.45 A, which is the ideal-transformer value.

stem: Electric power is transmitted over long distances at very high voltage mainly because
options: the current, and so I²R loss, is smaller
explanation: For a fixed power P = VI, a higher V means a smaller I, and the heat lost in the cables, I²R, falls as the square of the current. Transformers are exactly what make the high voltage possible, and the frequency is unchanged.

stem: A power station sends 100 kW at 10 kV through cables of total resistance 5 Ω. The power lost as heat in the cables is
explanation: The line current is I = P/V = 100000/10000 = 10 A, so the loss is I²R = 100 × 5 = 500 W. Using V²/R with the full 10 kV gives 2 × 10⁷ W, but 10 kV is not the voltage across the cables.

stem: The peak value of an alternating voltage is 200√2 V. Its rms value is
explanation: For a sinusoidal voltage V_rms = V₀/√2 = 200√2/√2 = 200 V. The value 100√2 V comes from dividing by 2 instead of √2.

stem: The rms value of an alternating current is 5 A. Its peak value is
explanation: I₀ = √2 × I_rms = 5√2 A, about 7.1 A. The value 2.5√2 A results from dividing by √2 instead of multiplying.

stem: An alternating voltage is given by V = 100 sin(100πt) volts. Its rms value and frequency are
explanation: Comparing with V₀ sin ωt: V₀ = 100 V, so V_rms = 100/√2 = 50√2 V, and ω = 100π gives f = ω/2π = 50 Hz. Reading 100 Hz directly from 100π confuses ω with f.

stem: For a 50 Hz alternating current, the time taken for the current to rise from zero to its peak value is
explanation: The period is T = 1/50 = 20 ms, and the current goes from zero to peak in a quarter cycle, T/4 = 5 ms. The value 10 ms is half a cycle, from zero back to zero.

stem: The average value of a sinusoidal alternating voltage of peak V₀ over one complete cycle is
explanation: The positive and negative half cycles are equal and opposite, so the average over a full cycle is zero. 2V₀/π is the average over a half cycle only, and V₀/√2 is the rms value.

stem: In a purely inductive AC circuit, the current compared with the applied voltage
explanation: The self-induced emf opposes changes in current, so the current reaches its maximum a quarter cycle after the voltage: it lags by 90° (π/2). Leading by 90° is the behaviour of a pure capacitor.

stem: In a purely capacitive AC circuit, the current
options: is in phase with the voltage
explanation: Current I = C dV/dt is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, that is when V passes through zero, so the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage: it leads by π/2. Lagging by π/2 describes a pure inductor.

stem: An alternating voltage is V = 200 sin(100πt) volts. Its instantaneous value at t = 1/600 s is
explanation: At t = 1/600 s, 100πt = π/6, so V = 200 sin 30° = 200 × ½ = 100 V. Using cos 30° gives 100√3 V.

stem: A sinusoidal current of peak value 4 A flows through a 10 Ω resistor. The average power dissipated is
explanation: I_rms = 4/√2 = 2√2 A, so P = I_rms²R = 8 × 10 = 80 W. Using the peak current gives I₀²R = 160 W, which is the maximum instantaneous power, not the average.

stem: The inductive reactance of a coil of inductance 0.1/π H in a 50 Hz supply is
explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 0.1/π = 10 Ω. Forgetting the factor 2 gives 5 Ω.

stem: The reactance of a capacitor of capacitance 100/π μF in a 50 Hz supply is
explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 50 × 10⁻⁴/π) = 1/0.01 = 100 Ω. Slipping a power of ten when converting 100 μF to 10⁻⁴ F gives 10 Ω or 1000 Ω.

stem: When the frequency of the AC supply is increased, the reactance of a capacitor
explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC), so the reactance is inversely proportional to frequency and falls as f rises. An inductor behaves the opposite way, with X_L = 2πfL rising with frequency.

stem: Which component blocks steady DC but allows AC to pass?
explanation: For DC, f = 0, so X_C = 1/(2πfC) is infinite and a capacitor blocks it, while for AC its reactance is finite. An inductor or choke does the reverse: X_L = 0 for DC.

stem: A series circuit has a resistance of 30 Ω and an inductive reactance of 40 Ω. Its impedance is
explanation: The voltages across R and L are 90° out of phase, so Z = √(R² + X_L²) = √(900 + 1600) = 50 Ω. Adding them directly to get 70 Ω ignores the phase difference.

stem: A 60 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 80 Ω are connected in series across a 200 V rms supply. The rms current is
explanation: Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, so I = 200/100 = 2 A. Adding R and X_C to 140 Ω gives 1.4 A, which ignores the phase difference.

stem: In a series RL circuit the resistance equals the inductive reactance. The phase relation between current and supply voltage is
explanation: tan φ = X_L/R = 1, so φ = 45°, and in an inductive circuit the current lags the voltage. A lag of 90° occurs only for a pure inductor with R = 0.

stem: A series RLC circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 80 Ω and X_C = 50 Ω. Its impedance is
explanation: X_L and X_C are opposite in phase, so the net reactance is 80 − 50 = 30 Ω, and Z = √(40² + 30²) = 50 Ω. Adding R to the net reactance gives 70 Ω, and adding everything gives 170 Ω.

stem: In a series RLC circuit, the rms voltages across the resistor, inductor and capacitor are 30 V, 60 V and 20 V. The rms supply voltage is
explanation: V_L and V_C are 180° apart, so their net is 60 − 20 = 40 V, at 90° to V_R: V = √(30² + 40²) = 50 V. Simply adding the three readings to get 110 V ignores the phases.

stem: A series circuit contains an inductor of 0.1 H and a capacitor of 10 μF. Its resonant frequency is
explanation: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) with LC = 0.1 × 10⁻⁵ = 10⁻⁶, so √(LC) = 10⁻³ s and f₀ = 1000/(2π) = 500/π Hz, about 159 Hz. The value 1000/π Hz forgets the 2 in 2π.

stem: At resonance, the impedance of a series RLC circuit is
explanation: At resonance X_L = X_C, so the reactances cancel and Z = √(R² + 0) = R, the minimum value, giving maximum current. It is a parallel resonant circuit, not a series one, whose impedance is maximum.

stem: The power factor of a series RLC circuit at resonance is
explanation: At resonance the net reactance is zero, current and voltage are in phase (φ = 0) and cos φ = R/Z = 1. A power factor of 0 belongs to a purely reactive circuit.

stem: The average power consumed by an ideal inductor connected to an AC supply is
explanation: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ and for an ideal inductor φ = 90°, so cos φ = 0 and P = 0. Energy stored in the field during one quarter cycle is returned to the supply in the next.

stem: In an AC circuit, V_rms = 220 V, I_rms = 5 A and the current lags the voltage by 60°. The average power consumed is
explanation: P = V_rms I_rms cos φ = 220 × 5 × cos 60° = 1100 × 0.5 = 550 W. The value 1100 W ignores the power factor, and 950 W uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°.

stem: A 60 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 80 Ω are in series across a 100 V rms supply. The average power consumed by the circuit is
explanation: Z = √(60² + 80²) = 100 Ω, so I_rms = 1 A. Only the resistor dissipates power: P = I²R = 1 × 60 = 60 W (equivalently VI cos φ with cos φ = 0.6). The value 100 W is V_rms I_rms, which ignores the power factor.

stem: A coil of inductance 1/π H is connected in series with a capacitor. For the circuit to resonate at 50 Hz, the capacitance must be
explanation: X_L = 2π × 50 × 1/π = 100 Ω, and resonance needs X_C = 1/(2π × 50 × C) = 100 Ω, so C = 1/(10⁴π) F = 100/π μF. Checking 10/π μF gives X_C = 1000 Ω, which does not match X_L.

stem: In AC circuits a choke coil is preferred to a resistor for reducing current because
options: it wastes very little power as heat
it makes the power factor one
it stores charge on its turns
explanation: A choke has large inductive reactance but small resistance, so its power factor is close to zero and it limits the current while dissipating very little energy. A resistor would turn the dropped voltage into heat.

stem: In a series LC circuit the inductance is made four times larger while the capacitance is unchanged. The resonant frequency becomes
explanation: f₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)) ∝ 1/√L, so multiplying L by 4 divides f₀ by √4 = 2. 'A quarter' forgets the square root.

stem: A pure inductor of inductance 1.1/π H is connected to a 220 V rms, 50 Hz supply. The rms current is
explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × 50 × 1.1/π = 110 Ω, so I = 220/110 = 2 A. Forgetting the factor 2 in 2πf gives X_L = 55 Ω and 4 A.

stem: In a series RC circuit across a 100 V rms supply, the rms voltage across the resistor is 80 V. The rms voltage across the capacitor is
explanation: V² = V_R² + V_C², so V_C = √(100² − 80²) = √3600 = 60 V. Subtracting directly to get 20 V ignores the 90° phase difference between V_R and V_C.

stem: A series RL circuit with R = 80 Ω has an inductive reactance of 30 Ω at 50 Hz. Its impedance at 100 Hz is
explanation: X_L = 2πfL is proportional to f, so at 100 Hz X_L = 60 Ω and Z = √(80² + 60²) = 100 Ω. About 85 Ω is the impedance at 50 Hz, forgetting that the reactance doubles.

stem: The rms value of an alternating current is
options: the mean of all instantaneous values
the steady current giving the same heating
the value at one quarter of the period
explanation: The rms value is the steady (DC) current that produces heat at the same rate in a given resistor; for a sine wave it equals I₀/√2. The mean of the instantaneous values over a cycle is zero, so it cannot measure the effect of AC.

stem: A series RLC circuit with R = 30 Ω, X_L = 70 Ω and X_C = 30 Ω is connected to a 100 V rms supply. The average power consumed is
explanation: Z = √(30² + (70 − 30)²) = 50 Ω, so I_rms = 2 A and P = I²R = 4 × 30 = 120 W. The value 200 W is V_rms I_rms, which ignores the power factor cos φ = 30/50 = 0.6.

stem: A lamp in series with an air-cored coil glows on an AC supply. A soft iron rod is slowly pushed into the coil. The lamp
explanation: The iron core greatly increases the inductance L, so X_L = 2πfL and the impedance rise, the current falls and the lamp dims. It does not go out, since the impedance stays finite and some current still flows; 'brighter' would need the impedance to fall.

stem: A long straight wire carries a current of 20 A. The magnetic field at 5 cm from it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 20/0.05 = 8 × 10⁻⁵ T. Leaving r as 5 instead of 0.05 m gives 8 × 10⁻⁷ T, and using the loop formula μ₀I/(2r) gives about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ T.

stem: A long solenoid has 1000 turns per metre. The current needed to produce a field of 2π × 10⁻³ T inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m/A)
explanation: I = B/(μ₀n) = 2π × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 1000) = 2π × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁴) = 5 A. Inverting the ratio of the π terms gives 2 A.

stem: A wire 2 m long carries 3 A towards the north in a uniform magnetic field of 5 × 10⁻⁵ T that also points north. The magnetic force on the wire is
explanation: F = BIL sin θ and here the current is parallel to the field, so θ = 0° and F = 0. The value 3 × 10⁻⁴ N is BIL, which would apply only if the wire were perpendicular to the field.

stem: An electron moves in a circle in a uniform magnetic field. Which quantity remains constant?
explanation: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work and the speed, and so the kinetic energy, stays constant. Velocity, momentum and acceleration are vectors whose directions keep changing around the circle.

stem: An electron (mass 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg, charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves at 4 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ T. The radius of its path is
explanation: r = mv/(eB) = (9 × 10⁻³¹ × 4 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 4.5 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.6 × 10⁻²⁴/7.2 × 10⁻²³ = 0.05 m = 5 cm. A slip of one power of ten in the numerator gives 0.5 cm or 50 cm.

stem: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 2 mA. The series resistance needed to convert it into a voltmeter of range 0-20 V is
explanation: The total resistance must be 20/0.002 = 10000 Ω, so the series resistance is 10000 − 50 = 9950 Ω. Choosing 10000 Ω forgets the galvanometer's own 50 Ω, and 10050 Ω adds it instead of subtracting.

stem: A galvanometer of resistance 20 Ω gives full-scale deflection at 5 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0-1 A is approximately
explanation: S = IgG/(I − Ig) = 0.005 × 20/0.995 ≈ 0.1/1 = 0.1 Ω. The shunt must be much smaller than G because it carries almost all of the 1 A; 4 Ω would let far too much current through the coil.

stem: A coil is held at rest in a strong but steady magnetic field. The emf induced in the coil is
explanation: Induced emf depends on the rate of change of flux linkage, ε = −NΔΦ/Δt. A steady field and a stationary coil give no change in flux, so the emf is zero however strong the field is. NBA is the flux linkage, not an emf.

stem: A metal rod 0.25 m long moves at 8 m/s at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T, with the rod perpendicular to both. The emf between its ends is
explanation: ε = BLv = 0.5 × 0.25 × 8 = 1 V. Leaving out the rod length gives 4 V, which would be the emf per metre of rod.

stem: A square loop of side 0.1 m and resistance 0.5 Ω is pulled at a steady 2 m/s out of a uniform magnetic field of 0.4 T that is perpendicular to the loop. One side is outside the field and the opposite side is still inside. The induced current is
explanation: Only the side still in the field cuts flux: ε = BLv = 0.4 × 0.1 × 2 = 0.08 V, so I = 0.08/0.5 = 0.16 A. The value 0.08 is the emf in volts, not the current.

stem: An emf of 12 V is induced in a coil when the current through it changes at 40 A/s. The self-inductance of the coil is
explanation: ε = L ΔI/Δt, so L = 12/40 = 0.3 H. Dividing 40 by 12 gives 3.3 H, and multiplying gives 480 H; neither follows from L = ε/(ΔI/Δt).

stem: An inductor of 2 H stores 25 J of energy in its magnetic field. The current through it is
explanation: U = ½LI², so I² = 2U/L = 50/2 = 25 and I = 5 A. Stopping at I² = 25 and giving 25 A forgets the square root.

stem: An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. Its primary has 1000 turns. The number of secondary turns is
explanation: Nₛ = Nₚ × Vₛ/Vₚ = 1000 × 12/240 = 50 turns. Using the ratio the wrong way gives 20000 turns, which would make a step-up transformer.

stem: A small DC motor runs on a 24 V supply and draws 3 A. Its armature resistance is 2 Ω. The back emf is
explanation: V = ε_b + IR, so ε_b = 24 − 3 × 2 = 18 V. The value 6 V is only the IR drop across the armature, and 30 V adds that drop to the supply.

stem: The rms value of the mains voltage in Pakistan is 220 V. Its peak value is about (√2 ≈ 1.41)
explanation: V₀ = √2 × V_rms = 1.41 × 220 ≈ 311 V. Dividing by √2 gives 156 V, which is backwards: the peak is larger than the rms value.

stem: An inductor has a reactance of 50 Ω at 50 Hz. Its reactance at 200 Hz is
explanation: X_L = 2πfL ∝ f, so multiplying the frequency by 4 multiplies the reactance by 4: 50 × 4 = 200 Ω. The value 12.5 Ω would be correct for a capacitor, whose reactance falls with frequency.

stem: A 40 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 30 Ω are in series across an AC supply. The power factor of the circuit is
explanation: Z = √(40² + 30²) = 50 Ω and power factor cos φ = R/Z = 40/50 = 0.8. The value 0.6 is X_C/Z, which is sin φ, not cos φ.

stem: A series RLC circuit with R = 10 Ω and L = 0.1 H is driven at its resonant angular frequency of 1000 rad/s by a 50 V rms supply. The rms voltage across the inductor is
explanation: At resonance Z = R, so I = 50/10 = 5 A. X_L = ωL = 1000 × 0.1 = 100 Ω, so V_L = 5 × 100 = 500 V. This is larger than the supply because V_L and V_C cancel each other; assuming V_L cannot exceed the supply leads to 50 V.

stem: Positive ions pass undeflected through crossed fields E = 2 × 10⁴ V/m and B = 0.1 T. They then enter a region of the same magnetic field alone and move in a circle of radius 5 cm. Their charge-to-mass ratio q/m is
explanation: The selector gives v = E/B = 2 × 10⁴/0.1 = 2 × 10⁵ m/s. In the field alone r = mv/(qB), so q/m = v/(Br) = 2 × 10⁵/(0.1 × 0.05) = 4 × 10⁷ C/kg. Using r = 5 instead of 0.05 m changes the result by a factor of 100 and is wrong.

stem: The coil of an AC generator rotates at 3000 revolutions per minute. The frequency of the emf it produces is
explanation: One revolution gives one complete cycle of emf, so f = 3000/60 = 50 revolutions per second = 50 Hz. Using 3000 Hz forgets to convert minutes to seconds.
